message.content:
Yes—**sports can help make a nation**, but not by themselves. They can strengthen **shared identity**, **national pride**, and even reduce some ethnic or social divisions, especially when people rally around a national team in major events like the World Cup or Olympics.[1][3]

The strongest evidence in your results comes from research on African national teams: victories in the Africa Cup of Nations were associated with weaker ethnic identification, better attitudes toward other ethnic groups, more trust and interaction across groups, and reduced inter-ethnic violence.[1] The same study found that a victory corresponded with a **37% drop** in the probability of someone reporting a strong ethnic identity, and that the effect was larger when the team was more ethnically diverse.[1]

That said, sports are better understood as a **tool for nation-building** than as a complete solution. They can create a temporary “we” feeling, offer symbols and stories that help define nationhood, and open a window for political dialogue or reform, but those effects may not last on their own.[1][3] In other words, sports can **support** nationhood; they usually cannot **create** a stable nation without institutions, politics, and shared civic rules.
